# What Snapback 4 Does Not Do

Longer than the doing-list on purpose. Moving something off it means writing one
line naming what it unblocks and taking something off the doing-list in the same
change. Nothing comes off during slice one (LLP 3000 §3: the clock is four weeks).

## The bars

The bakeoff gates in [LLP 3000 §3](../llp/3000-snapback4.explainer.md) are the
bars: the loop bar, hub acquisition within 2× the measured floor, client bytes
under the competitor-anchored budgets, the six scenarios green in the simulator
on the hub fixture. Everything not required to pass them does not exist yet.

## Not building

- **A second authoring language.** Quarry, one spelling, copied from Snapback 2 (LLP 1004, LLP 1007 §4b). TypeScript is for seeds, journeys, effect bodies and the client.
- **Byte- and step-priced certification.** No closure, heap, output or step ceilings at `check`; the certificate certifies shape, uniformity, completeness class and prediction eligibility. Resources are metered at runtime (LLP 2000.000 §6).
- **A per-query result cache.** No range receipts, validators, halos, absence evidence, coverage spans, extent facts, held directories, fact integrity or swap journals. The client replicates declared partitions with one watermark each (LLP 2000.000 §7).
- **Engine-minted ids for client inserts, grants, ID slices.** Ids are client-minted, time-ordered, 128-bit; the engine mints for its own writes.
- **The `drain` protocol, follower-tab inbox rows, `defineItems`, `withHistory`, `mutationTarget`, `receipt.source`, `local.caughtUp`, `partial` reason codes.** The card (`packages/snapback4/src/contract.ts`) is the whole client vocabulary; `why` carries the rest.
- **`retain` as a receipt rule.** `until-revoked` and `delivered-history` survive as the client's leave policy on a scope tombstone.
- **JavaScript in the data plane.** Queries and mutations run in the Rust interpreter inside the SQLite transaction, and in the same interpreter on the client (host decided at week 3 by measurement, LLP 2000.000 §9). A *job* may be the app's own Rust, hosted as wasm through the interpreter's operations under the job's meter (LLP 3000.005, the Moves line below); a query or mutation may not.
- **An embedded JS engine for effects.** The data plane never calls out. `emit` writes the effect durably in the mutation's commit and an external worker holding a service token claims, performs and settles it over the wire (`snapback4/worker`); the four reference effects run on the builder's Node (LLP 2000.000 §10, decided 2026-09-13).
- **Committed generated code; an auth mode; a supervised bundler.** As Snapback 2 (`rules/NOT-DOING.md`): types by inference, personas not modes, `SNAPBACK_URL` is the client contract.
- **A TypeScript twin of the interpreter.** Retired by the author's ruling of 2026-09-13 (LLP 3000 §7): one implementation, in Rust, on every host — the core's SQLite under the native module, memory under wasm on the web with the host persisting each commit's changes. The web pays 312,924 B gzip before the diet where the twin's tier paid 16,842; the conformance obligation between two interpreters ends. Expo Go runs the online tier.
- **More than one hosted target, an admin console, media transcoding or thumbnails, push delivery itself (a worker's), cron syntax beyond `every N at HH:MM`, vector or relevance-ranked search (word-prefix search is in: `words(..)` and `matching`), federation, multi-region, device-to-device sync, at-rest encryption claims.** After the clock, on evidence.
- **General observability beyond `why`, `trace`, `logs`, `data`, `sql`, server operation latency, and bounded client subscription inspection.** The `sql` verb is read-only inspection of the developer's own store (LLP 3000.007 §8.8), never an application surface. Separately declared application SQL reads are admitted for increment D (LLP 3000.009 §6.2, §14.4; the 2026-09-16 Moves line below), not implemented by this inspection verb.
- **A guide corpus.** The compiler's facts, one language card and keyword cards, as Snapback 2; no freshness dates. Every card's Quarry is compiled by the suite and the language card is run, so a card cannot promise a form the parser refuses.

- **Partial union delivery, two group audiences, a public branch.** A union syncs principal-column branches and at most one group branch, each a whole disjunct of the read rule (LLP 3000.036.000.000); a branch with an extra condition, a second group or a `public` branch is refused with the rewrite, never partially delivered; service grants add no device audience (LLP 3000.007 §20.6). A union does not combine with delivered history, read-through children, synced or row-keyed views, owner keys, timelines, private field owners, acquisition windows or direct/inherited expiry on content or membership scopes.
- **Exact horizon maintenance.** The horizon bounds acquisition (a snapshot, a bootstrap); the log never evicts or back-fills to hold a device's group at exactly N rows. A local read past the acquired horizon by key says `complete: false`.

- **Clock expressions in rules.** A read rule compares with `=` and `!=` only; `.expiresAt > now` remains a mutation `require`. Stored lifetimes use `not before .col` for server-controlled opening and `expire at .col` for expiry. The engine publishes opening commits; devices receive no unopened payload. The supported compositions and explicit exclusions are in LLP 3000.036.003.
- **A jobs framework.** No priorities, worker pools or dead letters: one FIFO of runs, one chunk at a time, a refused chunk parked with its refusal. Actions, effects and scheduled actions carry per-operation retries, deadlines and cancellation, and a record per external step (LLP 3000.009 §5.2; the Moves line below). Missed period boundaries while a server is down fire once on return, not once per missed period.
- **Asset processing.** No transcoding, thumbnails, rungs or HEIC: the bytes are served as uploaded; JPEG, PNG, WebP and MP4 only; image dimensions and optional MP4 duration read from the header; MP4 dimensions are not extracted.
- **Search beyond word prefixes.** One tokenizer (NFC, lowercase, alphanumeric words), one index shape (`scope, words(cols), order.., id`), one read (`matching`): every term a prefix of some word, the first term's words merged as lanes, bounded by the meter in a uniform scope, at most 32 words in an admitted non-uniform scope. No stemming, no ranking by relevance, no phrase or mid-word matching, no per-language folding, no intersection index for the second term (it filters the page).
- **An identity provider.** Guests, password accounts, service seats, and sessions a service mints for accounts the application authenticated itself. No phone, OAuth, magic links or MFA in the engine: an application's worker verifies those and mints the session.
- **No multi-server presence, no presence history or last-seen storage, no broadcast event stream, no connection-bound rows.** `connected[p]` stays server-wide, counting held polls and their 35 s grace; a live query that may read it re-runs in the background about every 5 seconds to stay current (LLP 3000.018). Typing and viewing use short-lived, authorized ephemeral tables in one server process (LLP 3000.017); they never sync or decide durable invariants. A device does not know presence and says so.

## Process not doing

- **2026-09-28 — ordinary mixed search** (LLP 3000.028 §3.3, lane OS round 1).
  Admit the SDK's bounded merge of current server rows and certified Left images
  for the proved single time-ordered word page. This removes application-owned
  online/held selection for that shape. One server call per requested page;
  recomputation pays again from consumed positions. The coordinator shares the
  existing device read allowance. No durable search session, extra synced rows,
  new authority or additional allowance is admitted.

- **2026-09-28 — inferred current-scope word search** (LLP 3000.028 §3.3,
  lane OS). A single bare ordinary word page may derive the exact non-expiring
  membership audience for the existing compact server plan. This removes the
  requirement to repeat that audience predicate in this narrow server query.
  The compiler supplies a scoped words index when absent; it is an ordinary
  schema index, maintained on writes and on devices, with no extra synced rows
  or new authority. The device keeps its original bare scan. Round 0 left ordered composition
  and combined accounting outside its independent subset; round 1 above admits
  that bounded SDK composition. Durable search sessions remain excluded.
- **2026-10-12 — union sync audiences** (LLP 3000.036.000.000, workstream UNION, two blind review rounds). A table syncs to the union of principal-column audiences and one group audience; a device holds a row while any branch admits its viewer. What it unblocks: owner-or-team, buyer-or-seller and owner-or-staff tables offline for every reader, the shape three app farms asked for. Taken off: "one `sync` audience per table". Partial delivery, two groups and a public branch stay excluded (above).
- **2026-09-28 — explicit owner-key coverage** (LLP 3000.028 §3.4, Lane OK commission). A public window may opt into a compiler-owned, horizon-free principal key partition to answer ordinary own-key existence offline. Taken off: the exclusion of narrower platform key distribution beside one public window. General union audiences, full own-row replication and per-query absence caches remain excluded. The projection uses existing metered maintains, adoption and whole-partition publication; existing windows do not expand.
- **2026-09-26 — a live query keeps presence current** (LLP 3000.018). A 0.4.2 probe found an observed `connected[p]` reporting `fresh: true` while stale for over a minute, and a comparative builder polled around it. What it unblocks: online marks and presence-aware lists that stay current. Taken off: "a presence stream" as an exclusion for live queries; a presence API, last-seen storage and multi-server presence stay out. Under the author's standing authorization for reworks that make queries excellent (2026-09-25).

- **No drift registries, inventories, line-pinned diagnostics registries, claim digests or frozen-record gates.** Generated projections are built, not committed.
- **No gate bound to an exact commit; no push gated on a battery.** Five blocking checks in sixty seconds, run before push; everything slower on a schedule with bounded tickets.
- **No ceiling raised in slice one.** Budgets are anchored to a competitor's measured number and recorded once in the journal.
- **No standing panel** except the two blind reviews LLP 3000 decision 4 names (partition inversion; the meter's cut on non-uniform scans). The author explicitly commissioned the one-off LLP 3000.008 panel and disjoint Astra implementation lanes on 2026-09-14; its bounded disposition is recorded in that umbrella and LLP 3000 §7.
- **No new LLP number** without first extending LLP 3000 or LLP 2000.000; no spec without running code (`rules/RULES.md`: only implemented specs bind).
- **No second session on the core** during slice one; lanes take the periphery.
- **No test matrix as the primary harness.** The simulator is; real-browser and device witnesses cover only what it cannot reach.
- **No files over 1,500 lines**, including ones copied from Snapback 2. Split on
  the way in. The one exception is the package's published documents
  (`packages/snapback4/README.md` and its linked references): the rule exists to
  keep a *source* file reviewable, and the 0.2.25 calibration measured the cost of
  applying it to a document — splitting the README was that run's single largest
  scoring loss, because the builder then had four places to look instead of one
  (LLP 3000.007 §20.19). A published document is bounded by whether a builder can
  find one way in, not by a line count; the census that enforces this rule covers
  source, and says so.

## Deliberately worse

- No compatibility with Snapback 1 or Snapback 2 apps, packages or on-disk formats.
- No API stability before the clock; every publish is `0.0.x`.
- Sparse prose documentation; the diagnostics and the recipes carry the load.
- One hosted target, one platform binary at a time. SQLite remains the default store; Postgres as a production store is being built under LLP 3000.009.001 (Moves, 2026-10-20) and is not yet a supported deployment target.

## Moves

- **2026-10-20 — Snapback 4 on Postgres moves onto the doing-list** (author: "commit and push these things, then do your \"what i'd do next\" things, then get this working on postgres and measure it"; LLP 3000.009.001 and its children). Unblocks: the store-port extraction on SQLite (P0, including the `Committer` seam with the serial batch); the Postgres adapters for every durable-state family and `serve`/`deploy`/`doctor` over Postgres (P1), with store-held fencing, the declared HA mode and `BlobStore`; the optimistic committer, commissioned on 2026-10-19 and built after its execution stage is sized; the scale program of LLP 3000.009.001.002 with its raw-Postgres, Supabase and Convex controls on fleet machines; and a research note comparing replicated SQLite with Postgres for applications that outgrow one SQLite file. Taken off in the same change: the evaluation-only framing of the Postgres adapter. Stands: no publication or managed-service deployment authority, no lowering of Quarry to SQL, no SQL writes to managed data, one core owner. Several serving processes (P2), log retention, live graduation (LLP 3000.009.001.001) and the async-safe external anchor each wait for their own Moves line.

- **2026-10-13 — stored lower lifetimes (`not before`) are commissioned by PAGE2** (LLP 3000.036.003). This unblocks timed disclosure without an application publication job. Per-application jobs that flip a publication flag leave this admitted path; clock expressions in rules, captured lower lifetimes for read-through children, and boundary recounts for maintained data remain excluded. HS owns handshake transport; PAGE2 declares the new semantic capability.

- **2026-10-06 — exact Following history (FH delegated round-1 ruling).**
  Admit a Following-specific server traversal and bounded volatile frontier/replay
  state under LLP 3000.026 §9. The approved design reads exact history online
  from the first page; the SDK will own continuation. The first milestone is internal event metadata
  and the oracle, with no public completeness claim. Taken off: a blanket ban on
  state for this one expiring read. General result caches, resumable queries,
  device traversal, inbox coverage certificates and history-only blocks remain
  excluded. Existing inbox bytes and runtime ceilings remain unchanged.

- **2026-09-26 — server operation latency (LLP 3000.019 §3.7).** Calibration #22
  measured each read once and could not claim repeated p95/degradation testing.
  Unblocks percentile measurements of the application's own load without a
  custom timing harness. Taken off: a latency harness written by the builder;
  general metrics, tracing infrastructure and an admin console remain excluded.

- **2026-09-23 — Quarry states intent moves onto the doing-list** (Charlie:
  "if you need to try making *significant* architectural reworks in order to
  make the data modeling, queries, and scalability be excellent and elegant,
  you can experiment with that"; LLP 3000.013). Unblocks reads that state
  predicates and order, one `view` declaration for derived data, Following
  without caps, jobs and aggregates without author-chosen bounds, an app
  object and an offline web shell. Taken off: index names and author-chosen
  engine numbers on the paved path; the timeline's promotion, pull routes and
  caps; the "Time in rules" refusal is unchanged. Stands: one interpreter, no
  JavaScript in the data plane, no lowering Quarry to SQL, no relevance-ranked
  search.

- **2026-09-16 — the remaining general-purpose program moves onto the doing-list**
  (Charlie: "complete everything ... we'll remove services when we are done
  with the workroom test rather than wait to add them in ... use the fleet";
  LLP 3000.009 §14.7). Unblocks the §7 integrated-service baseline, C3 production
  Postgres, D's authorized database capabilities and measurement-led C2/E
  work while Workroom continues. Taken off: waiting for Workroom before
  starting services, and keeping production Postgres integration outside the
  current implementation program. The completed Workroom record drives a
  retain/remove pass. Stands: one interpreter and managed writer, no managed
  SQL writes, no JavaScript transactions, no SQL in the first Workroom cell,
  no invented performance/real-provider evidence, no expo-build-1000 load,
  and no new publication or managed-service deployment authority.

- **2026-09-16 — application SQL reads move onto the doing-list** (Charlie: "admit application SQL reads"; LLP 3000.009 §6.2, §14.4, increment D). Unblocks reporting and search over authorized projection inputs and declared database-owned tables, with authorization before selection, ordering and limits. Taken off in the same change: the inspection-only exclusion for application SQL and D's pending-author gate. Implementation and qualification remain pending; SQLite and Postgres halves ship together, channels follow candidates, and A1–A3 plus the fixture pack stay first. Stands: no SQL writes into managed data, no lowering Quarry to SQL, no SQL in the first Snapback brief cell, and no publication authorization.

- **2026-09-15 — a Postgres evaluation backend moves onto the doing-list** (author: "Build the evaluation prototype"). Unblocks concrete evaluation of storage agnosticism, interpreter/database round trips and transactional sync ordering. This bounded prototype replaces full CLI/deployment integration as the next backend task; those product surfaces remain off this increment's doing-list. It shares Quarry, rules, maintains and partition logic, but uses an experimental Postgres store. Native SQL exists only as an explicitly separate comparison workload, not an application escape hatch. SQLite remains the production and local-device store. See [the experiment](./experiments/postgres/README.md).

- **2026-09-15 — the server half of LLP 3000.009 moves onto the doing-list** (author: "begin implementation using astra xhigh to code"; LLP 3000.009 §10.2, increments A1–A3). Unblocks the online-only brief's invitation, webhook and scheduled journeys without a second application server: work records whose authority is bound at admission, ids bound to their operation and arguments, declared action results, a generated handler context with a durable record per external step, declared routes and webhooks, scheduled actions under service seats, and `serve` supervising the runtime. Taken off in the same change: "A jobs framework" narrows — actions, effects and scheduled actions get per-operation retries, deadlines and cancellation; priorities, worker pools and dead letters stay out — and the actions card's "supervise the worker as an ordinary Node process" leaves. Stands: no JavaScript in the data plane, no identity provider in the engine, and no `ctx.sql`, projections or SQL reads in this increment.

- **2026-09-15 — the Postgres access boundary moves onto the doing-list** (LLP 3000.009 §10.2, increment C1). Unblocks measuring Postgres behind a batched access boundary instead of row-at-a-time calls: transaction-scoped prefetch, a pipelined commit tail, one portable index-key bound checked on both stores, and the corpus, conformance and device suites on both stores. Taken off in the same change: the evaluation prototype's single-adapter framing, in which the only next step was an unbatched store. Stands: Postgres is not a hosted or deployable target; its refusals of assets, jobs, actions and schedules, and `serve`, `deploy` and backup on Postgres, wait for increment C3.

- **2026-09-13 — word search, effects, service seats and presence move onto the doing-list** (author: "add all the things we need for Clique and Interview"; the full-brief Clique record's remaining capability lines and Interview's adapter responsibilities). What it unblocks: Clique M5's three search scopes online and offline on one index, M6's push seam without connection leases hand-built in tables, M8's digest emitted rather than logged into a table, Interview's phone sign-in and model workers as a service that mints sessions instead of proxying every request, and the ranked feed of LLP 3000.004 on the `feeds` card. Taken off in the same change: "an embedded JS engine for effects, until measured" (the engine never calls out; a worker does), "word search" from the package's exclusions. Stands: no JavaScript in the data plane, no relevance ranking, no identity provider in the engine.
- **2026-09-12 — expiry, assets and jobs move onto the doing-list** (author: "complete snapback4 to the point where the entire clique benchmark can be run"). What it unblocks: the struck half of the Clique brief (M4 media, M5 view-once and expiry with no client open, M8's scheduled digest). Taken off in the same change: the "one photo path" and "cron syntax" exclusions above narrow to transcoding and to cron beyond `every N [at HH:MM]`; the "time in rules" exclusion stands, answered by `expire at .col` rather than a rule.
- **2026-09-13 — native jobs on (author: "write up an LLP about this and then implement").** Unblocks the scoring half of a feed — floats, vectors, real loops, a typed schema — without putting any of it into Quarry, and gives the model half of LLP 3000.004 a seat inside the bounds: one chunk per commit, the job ceilings, fuel, no I/O. Off the doing-list in the same change: the "external ranker with a service seat" of LLP 3000.004 §6.5 is no longer the only shape for compute over the store; it remains the shape for the network. - **2026-09-13 — `sql`, a fifth named observability verb, moves onto the doing-list** (author ruling on LLP 3000.007 §14.10). ## Summary

Snapback 4 is one of two parallel candidates for the successor to Snapback 2,
and the sibling of Snapback 3, not its successor. It builds
[LLP 2000.000](./2000.000-keep-the-core-flip-two-substrates.rfc.md) as
written: the Snapback 2 core kept verbatim, two substrates flipped up front —
resources metered at runtime instead of priced statically, and a client that
replicates the viewer's declared partition instead of caching receipted
results — proved first on the hub fixture, with a deterministic simulator as
the primary harness. Snapback 3 ([LLP 2000](./2000-snapback3.rfc.md), led by
Codex / GPT-6 Astra) keeps the same two questions open and discovers their
answers in its first slice. Snapback 2 ([LLP 1000](./1000-snapback2.explainer.md))
continues as the incumbent and the control. All three are judged by one
pre-registered comparison on one clock.

This document records the author's decisions of 2026-09-12 that created the
track, restates the bet on one page so a reader can orient without the brief,
fixes the bakeoff protocol, draws the fence, and plans the first four weeks.
The design argument and its evidence stay in LLP 2000.000. Only running code
will bind (`rules/RULES.md`).

## 1. Decisions (author, 2026-09-12)

On 2026-09-12 Charlie Cheever asked whether Claude Fable 5.1 should lead a
Snapback 4 while Codex / GPT-6 Astra leads Snapback 3 and Snapback 2
continues, "and see which one turns out best." The lead answered yes with
conditions; the author accepted them ("Sounds good") and asked for this
document. The decisions below are therefore the lead's proposal as accepted
by the author. Where the author has not separately ruled, the text says so.

1. **Three tracks, one comparison.** Snapback 2 continues as the incumbent
   and the control. Snapback 3 builds LLP 2000; Snapback 4 builds LLP
   2000.000. This is a bakeoff of *bets* — discover the substrates in the
   slice versus decide them first — not of models. The result will say more
   about the bets than about the leads, and §3 is written so that it can.
2. **The name is Snapback 4.** Siblings, not a sequence: "4" does not mean
   "after 3." A separate number gives the track its own corpus root,
   directory, package identity and data directory with no rename when the
   bakeoff resolves, and files never move in LLP. If Snapback 4 loses, it is
   a number that never shipped. "Snapback 3b" was considered and rejected:
   it reads as a variant of 3, and this is a different bet.
3. **Snapback 4 builds LLP 2000.000 as written.** Its §14 open questions are
   the lead's to decide inside the track, recorded in §7 as they are
   decided. The author rules on the bar, the comparison and promotion (§3).
4. **One owner on the core.** The lead writes the engine, the store and the
   client contract. Codex lanes build the fixture generator, the reference
   applications, the device witnesses and the periphery. Blind reviews from
   two model families are reserved for the two disclosure-sensitive
   mechanisms: partition inversion of read rules (LLP 2000.000 §7.1) and
   the meter's cut behaviour on non-uniform scans (LLP 2000.000 §6). This
   departs from the standing rule that Codex codes and Claude orchestrates,
   deliberately, for the core only.
5. **The clock is four weeks** from the first commit under `snapback4/` to
   the first slice running on the hub fixture. At the clock the author kills
   the track, merges its substrates into a survivor, or continues it. There
   is no third month without a ruling.
6. **Shared and not shared.** Shared with Snapback 3: the LLP corpus, the
   Clique harness and scorers, the fixtures, the briefs, and the simulator
   once either track has one. Not shared: code, except the Snapback 2 pieces
   both are expected to copy (LLP 2000.000 §5.1).
7. **Snapback 2 keeps shipping and freezes new substrate work for the
   duration.** Fix-forward, the loop bar, acquisition and papercuts continue;
   no new certificate axes, client custody mechanisms or ceiling changes.
   This is accepted here as a condition of the bakeoff. Making it binding on
   concurrent Snapback 2 sessions needs one line in `rules/NOT-DOING.md`'s
   Moves ledger, which this document does not write.
8. **Reading load.** This root, updated in place, and one append-only
   journal, `snapback4/JOURNAL.md`. Sub-LLPs only for a decision that must
   outlive the journal. No panels beyond decision 4's two reviews.

## 2. The bet on one page

**Keep verbatim from Snapback 2** (LLP 2000.000 §5.1): the rule language
with its uniformity and hoist analysis, `decided_true` and the
structural-fact refusals; one data language, Quarry, with `--` comments,
`require … else CODE`, `shape`, `merge`, `walk`, `chunk`; the value model
and its conformance corpus; typed read and write states with no silent state
and the refusal envelope `{code, family, site, message, rewrite, guide}`; the
successor classifier (widening additive, checked narrowing, exact projection
ownership); `deliver`'s engine-computed audience, tombstones and
`bootstrap`; `schedule`, `job`, `chunk` and rehearsal; personas; `init`,
`dev`, `check`, `doctor`, `run`, `test`, `why`, `trace`, `guide`; H0
`deploy`, `rollback`, `secret`; channels; assets; the word-prefix index.

**Flip 1 — certify authorization, meter resources** (LLP 2000.000 §6). The
certificate keeps every read site's shape, uniformity, completeness class
and prediction eligibility, and stops pricing bytes and steps. A
deterministic meter charges examined rows, index entries, rule probes,
steps, heap, output and rows written as the program runs, on the server and
in the client interpreter alike. A query cut by the meter returns `capped`
with no continuation past the cut, the same observable outcome as a static
ceiling cut today; a mutation aborts with `E_BOUND` naming actual work; a
job is chunked. `check --cost` prints the structural cost class; `test`
prints measured meters on the hub fixture.

**Flip 2 — the viewer's partition is the unit of sync** (LLP 2000.000 §7).
`sync to <audience> last N by <index>` on a table makes the engine maintain,
per principal, the rows that principal may read, as a change log with a
horizon; a table without the word is online-only, and `check` says which
rule term prevented inversion. The client holds a replica of its partitions,
one watermark each, a durable outbox with client-minted ids, and the
interpreter; queries run locally and are `complete` inside the horizon.
Revocation is a scope tombstone; `until-revoked` and `delivered-history`
survive as the client's leave policy. Two client tiers — online-only
without a store, local-first with one — share one language and one server.

**The vocabulary is fixed before the mechanism** (LLP 2000.000 §8):

```ts
type Read<T> = { data: T; complete: boolean; fresh: boolean; since?: number; next?: Cursor }
            | { loading: true } | { denied: Refusal };
row.pending: boolean;
type Write = { state: "pending" } | { state: "sent"; seq: number } | { state: "failed"; why: Refusal };
type Link = "online" | "offline" | "signed-out";
```

A screen that needs a word not on that card is a defect in the mechanism,
not a gap in the card.

**The hub comes first** (LLP 2000.000 §11): the Clique generator's `u0001`
with 1,000 memberships, `u0500` with 500 follows, and about 100,000
messages are the first fixture; day-two changes are designed before the
day-one screen; the native client is in slice one; physical floors are
measured before targets; the simulator is the primary harness.

## 3. The bakeoff protocol

Shared with Snapback 3; LLP 2000 or a sibling record should adopt the same
text so that the two tracks are measured by one instrument.

**Brief.** [`benchmarks/briefs/social-messenger.md`](../benchmarks/briefs/social-messenger.md)
(Clique) M1–M8, plus
[`benchmarks/briefs/messaging-day2-evolution.md`](../benchmarks/briefs/messaging-day2-evolution.md).
The field-work application (LLP 2000 §4) tests generality after the first
slice, on whichever tracks survive the clock.

**Fixture.** The Clique generator at the instrument freeze LLP 1023 and
LLP 1024 record (`f40559f37722c79178be664a11f8a6485f1508fd`): hub `u0001`
with 100 groups and 900 DMs, `u0500` with 500 follows, and the 100,015
messages of the retained 0.0.25 replay database. The same fixture for every
track and for the control.

**Harness and judge.** [`benchmarks/protocol.md`](../benchmarks/protocol.md);
the same three scorers as the 2026-09-05 run (gpt-6-astra, grok-4.6,
muse-spark); Convex as the control arm; published packages; fresh cold
agents with only the installed package and the task. Neither lead runs the
comparison or grades their own track. The author rules on the numbers.

**Decision rule, pre-registered.**

| Gate | Threshold | How measured |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loop bar | Fresh agent, published package, reduced Clique M1–M3, ≤ 1,200 s, ≤ 1 Snapback-attributed correction loop, N ≥ 3 | The existing loop-bar protocol (`rules/NOT-DOING.md` §"The bars") |
| Hub acquisition | Full durable content plus first offline thread and search on `u0001`, within 2× the measured physical floor | Floors recorded in the journal in week 1 (§5); the same script on every track |
| Client bytes | Online tier ≤ Convex's shipped React client; the local-first tier's JavaScript ≤ PowerSync's shipped web client, with the wasm device measured beside it and its own budget set by the diet (§7, 2026-09-13: one implementation) | Measured on one pinned toolchain, recorded once in the journal, never assumed |
| Scenarios | LLP 2000 §4's six scenarios green under the simulator on the hub fixture; LLP 2000 §10's outcomes 1–5 and LLP 2000.000 §11's 6–7 | The simulator run record plus the device witnesses |
| Interaction budgets | LLP 2000 §7's targets | Recorded beside the gates; descriptive, not gating, in slice one |
| Holistic score | Three-scorer Clique score with the Convex control | Reported; descriptive, not gating |

A track that passes every gate is a candidate for promotion. A track that
fails the loop bar or acquisition is killed at the clock unless the author
rules otherwise. A mixed result names the gains and the remaining costs, and
the author decides which substrates move into a survivor — which may be
Snapback 2 (LLP 2000.000 §13).

**Clock and checkpoints.** Week 1: floors, experience prototype, simulator
skeleton, first publish. Week 2: server core, partition stream, meter,
simulator invariants. Week 3: web replica, outbox, local queries, the chat
app on the real client. Week 4: Expo, day-two scenarios, deploy, the loop
bar, the Clique hub run, the comparison record. Four weeks from the first
commit.

## 4. Fence, numbering, routing

- **Directory.** `snapback4/`, with its own Cargo workspace and Bun
  workspace, excluded from the root workspace as `snapback2/` is. No
  Snapback 1 or Snapback 2 gate, inventory, backstop, registry or script
  applies; the pre-push hook selects none.
- **Identities.** Binary and npm shim `snapback4`; data directory
commits are 51195718c2 and 6b503b6730 on bf9c1ccc55; repair commits are
18027d335d and 40e0d0d91b. No further source changes were needed during
qualification. All Cargo commands were sequential, with at most four build
jobs, CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 and line-tables-only dev/test debug information.
The private-database scripts used RUST_TEST_THREADS=1; their contention
witnesses still create overlapping transactions internally. The default
core suite and host ratchets used four test threads. Sampled disk space
remained above the 15 GB stop threshold (32 GB free at final verification).

All three full scripts exit 0. Each reports 229 passed, zero failed and
zero ignored: 58 evaluation tests, 152 selected core Postgres tests and
19 corpus harness tests. Every one of the 24 Postgres asset cases runs and
passes in every script, including intermediate quota overflow with rollback,
signed stale-cutoff boundaries, all shape refusals and post-attach insert
suppression. The sibling identity, jobs, outbox and request persistence/rule
refusals all execute. Corpus exclusions remain named exclusions, not passes.

- PostgreSQL 16.15, C/C: /tmp/p1as-r1-pg16.log.
  Owned cluster: /tmp/sb4-pg-eval.qy9g2k.
- PostgreSQL 17.9, C/C, using SNAPBACK4_PG_SHARE for initdb -L:
  /tmp/p1as-r1-pg17.log. Owned cluster: /tmp/sb4-pg-eval.dAmSAe.
- PostgreSQL 16.15, en_US.utf8/en_US.utf8, using SNAPBACK4_PG_LOCALE:
  /tmp/p1as-r1-pg16-locale.log. Owned cluster: /tmp/sb4-pg-eval.wSfLRn.

Server queries confirm each version and locale. Every script confirms its
cluster stopped; a final independent pg_ctl status for all three returns 3,
and all three postmaster.pid files are absent. No other cluster was touched.
The serialized concurrency witness records 65 increments with zero retries
in each script; serializable also records 65 with no lost updates, using
63, 90 and 89 retries respectively. No retry bound or durability setting
changed.

The provided 17.9 server has zero pg_constraint rows with contype='n', even
with the installed NOT NULL ledger columns. Therefore the review's precise
NOT NULL-row reopen failure was not reproduced on this server. Assets and
outbox now explicitly ignore that constraint type as requested; identity
and jobs already filter primary/unique rows. Reopen and all refusal cases
pass on both actual server versions. A separate temporary-table probe also
confirms PostgreSQL forbids naming a non-view INSERT rule _RETURN; the
implicit-view-rule exception cannot hide a suppressing insert rule.

The full cargo test -p snapback4-core passes: 944 passed, zero failed, five
existing ignores, including all 17 doctests. The unit portion is 547 passed
and three ignored. The 45 printed result summaries include the isolated
one-test allocation-probe child; its pass is counted once in the 944 total.
Log: /tmp/p1as-r1-core.log. The focused asset run passes 27 SQLite/core cases
and reports the 24 named Postgres ignores without a database; the
legacy-NUL-home claim regression passes. Log: /tmp/p1as-r1-assets.log.

Both host ratchets pass unchanged: committer 3/3 and store-port 5/5.
Log: /tmp/p1as-r1-ratchets.log. The exact requested Clippy command reports
only the two inherited errors, while_immutable_condition at engine/read.rs:780
and never_loop at engine/row_views.rs:1013; neither file changed. A diagnostic
run allowing only those two lints completes all library/test checking with
no diagnostic in the new helpers or regression cases. Existing warnings
remain. Logs: /tmp/p1as-r1-clippy.log and
/tmp/p1as-r1-clippy-diagnostic.log. No source lint suppression was added.
Root ref-check and git diff --check pass; the final reference count is
recorded by /tmp/p1as-r1-refcheck.log. The RFC keeps its single Revised line
with P1-AS fix round 1 prepended and documents ordered asset_ids.

No push, stash, git configuration change, sub-agent, other worktree, remote
machine, new gate, allowance increase, publication or Postgres host wiring
was used. The remaining verification limitation is the absent contype='n'
catalog shape on the supplied 17.9 server, as recorded above.

## 12. Wave 14 authorization evidence and caller-gate lints

RULES4 keeps execution authority and public envelopes unchanged. A failed
explicit mutation `require` is identified as `mutation require` in developer
output, with its source clause and site. Table denials name `table <verb> rule`
and the original authored clause, preserving old/next phase attribution.
Generated asserted-lookups remain distinct program refusals and preserve the
hidden-read explanation. Local run, forwarded run and dev console use the
same captured generation's source metadata; forwarded output never quotes
current disk contents. Metadata lives only in the host's refusal-site map;
no clause text is added to Refusal, receipts, sync or production serve.

Extend the existing bounded rule-composition contradiction proof to direct
insert and delete writes. Keep N_WRITE_DENIED for proved impossible admitted
paths and deny/omitted rules. No unknown expression becomes a contradiction.
For a table write rule that is one keyed existence probe, N_REQUIRE_REFUSED
also identifies a mixed-OR require where one branch establishes that probe
and another does not. It is explicitly a **missing authority proof**, with a
possible refusal, never a claim that different roles are disjoint. A positive
caller-filtered program probe proves the same physical rule probe, including
additional equality tests; the reverse implication is never used. Normalize
named keys and unambiguous principal-typed viewer slots through real unique
indexes; raw-id/reference positional forms stay unknown instead of guessing
a unique ID-valued column. Compare known scalar/snapshot terms.
Another prior require establishing the probe on every branch suppresses it.
Drop these facts across writes, opaque calls, branches/rebindings that may
invalidate the witnessed rows; jobs remain exempt. Proved unreachable branches are discarded under the preceding path facts.
Unknown or oversized branch products stay quiet, with overflow propagated
through the complete expression. The advisory never changes admission or runtime.

The guide recipes cover a transactionally maintained mutable audience copy,
private waitlist/public occupancy, expiring membership pages, a union with an
explicit cold-start tradeoff, separate private/public image placements, and
own-or-staff queries. Execute exact shipped blocks against a packed consumer,
including revocation, expiry, unauthorized writes and asset home refusal.
A 100-schema before/after census must show no new refusals. LANG3 owns general
completeness notes; LLP 3000.014.000 owns live-parent design consequences.

### Language and note amendment: Wave 14 LANG3: surviving audiences and diagnostic consequence

Commissioned by Charlie Cheever on 2026-10-16 for 0.4.31. This amends
§10's source-diagnostic readability fragment, LLP 3000.036.001's completeness
reach, and LLP 3000.039's diagnostic presentation. Authorization recipes and
refusal-layer text belong to RULES4; null fixture aliases belong to KIT3.

**Captured parent proof.** A server query over an ordinary online table can
prove its page's read rule from a dominating, readable point snapshot and
its surviving control paths. A held point says that its read rule held at
that point; it does not say every child is readable. For example, after an
observer branch returns, a readable observation with `held = true` and
`read <- .observer = viewer or (.teacher = viewer and .held = true)` proves
that the remaining caller is its teacher. A child page pinning that exact
observation and its captured teacher can then prove
`.teacher = viewer and exists observations[.observation, held = true]`.
The page remains exactly the authored page; no filter, audience or order is
added or removed. The ordinary meter and page frontier remain in force.

The core independently rederives this sufficient proof from the program,
including externally supplied IR; no source-only marker grants authority.
It accepts read-only query bodies, once-bound point snapshots of total
unique keys from unchanged arguments/viewer/literals, positive row rules,
at most twelve independent propositional atoms and 1,024 formula nodes. Snapshot presence
implies its actual read rule. Unknown policy components contribute no
assumption; unknown positive child branches cannot help prove the goal.
The proof accounts for both conditional paths, requirements and early
returns. Rebinding, loops, expression blocks, pair-return sinks, mutation
bodies, copied audience conventions, read-through, maintenance, field owners,
lifetimes and synced outer tables do not establish this proof. A probe may
be witnessed only by the exact captured table/index/key and required field
values. Nullable Boolean false is never inferred from not-true. The setup of a lowered short-circuit temporary confers no completed-condition
facts. Nullable snapshot ids stay null in path comparisons; a positive
exact-key witness may equate its own id only together with its presence.
Interpreter-owned `$filter`/`$project` bindings confer no snapshot evidence.
Fresh-id evaluations, reads and builtins are not symbolic comparison
identities. A reconstructed short circuit may reference only once-bound
values; a reference to its own prior value or any other assigned temporary
declines this proof. Inconsistent path facts grant no trusted scan: the
sufficient implication must also have a satisfiable antecedent. Every scan
sharing an IR site must prove the verdict. Failure retains the existing
honest incomplete answer. This server-only analysis adds no IR/wire form or
device interpretation; local device coverage and authorization are unchanged.

**Finite flow facts.** Enum equality/inequality narrows the exact binding or
snapshot field. A true disjunction (or false conjunction) unions the
alternatives; it never assumes one alternative holds. Existing surviving-
branch joins carry the fact after a return/refusal. Rebinding and loop joins
retain their existing invalidation. Sorting a complete population is a
permutation and retains its original cap/uniformity proof; slicing, joining,
filtering or transforming a population does not gain that proof.

**Immutable patch diagnostics.** A conflict key that itself proves the read
rule (for example, owner pinned to viewer) now permits the same proven-change
and fresh-clock/id diagnostics as a public readable target. Lifetime and
hidden-target exclusions remain. Unknown argument timestamps remain notes;
an owner key for another principal cannot turn its hidden conflict into a
static inequality oracle. Exact local-insert/key equality still wins before
a clock diagnostic. An immutable field projected from the immutable parent
identified by an immutable, pinned target reference is treated as an
intentional stable equality guard and does not repeat N_IMMUTABLE_PATCH.
This is note suppression, not a storage-equality claim: historical rows still
undergo runtime equality, and no parent/child invariant is inferred. A mutable
parent field or unpinned parent identity keeps the note. All remaining
N_IMMUTABLE_PATCH notes are review notes that can cost correctness.

**Proven guard notes.** Proven independent roster facts survive unrelated
writes only when neither the target nor any of its read dependencies
was written. A delete includes the schema's complete cascade/set-null write
closure. Helpers, derived maintenance and row-derived evidence retain
conservative invalidation. N_LOOKUP_HIDDEN follows the actual read
proof at an actual required point-read gate. A blind mutable update is not
a program read and does not receive N_LOOKUP_HIDDEN merely because its table
write rule admits nonreaders. A required lookup names its actual refusal code;
its note is silent when earlier guards prove that exact row readable. Rebound,
wrong or volatile keys and effectful operands do not establish that witness.
A point update counts as an earlier target
lookup attempt for N_REFERENCE_UNCHECKED, just as a nullable point read does,
including through a known helper only when every successful path performs
that lookup. Silence of that note never proves existence or successful authorization.
These notes change neither authorization nor reference integrity. A reference still validates an id, not existence.
# Frontend data and actionable notes

**Type:** RFC
**Status:** Review
**Systems:** snapback4-client, snapback4-language, snapback4-cli
**Author:** Charlie Cheever (implementation by Codex)
**Date:** 2026-10-18
**Revised:** 2026-10-18
**Related:** LLP 3000.013 §6, LLP 3000.031, LLP 3000.036 §17, LLP 3000.040

## 1. Evidence and boundaries

Wave 16's paired bakeoff has frontend medians 200 and 75.5 nonblank
lines. Starter production examples count as frontend even when never imported.
The report attributes all 50 pairs using the unchanged harness buckets.
FRONT owns the additive React surface and completeness presentation here.
RULES5 owns refusing-clause traces and role implications; LANG4 owns other
notes; DAY5 owns starter adaptation; KIT4 owns clock caps and test sessions;
STAGE owns provisioning. SEC owns security invariants. No change to contract.ts,
authorization, completeness certificates or protocol is proposed here.

## 2. A short common read

Add `useQueryData(op, args, options?)` in `snapback4/react`, shared by React
and Expo. It delegates directly to `useQuery` and returns `R | undefined`:
loading gives undefined; present, absent and partial give their exact data
(including null, empty lists, false and zero). A denied read throws
`QueryRefusal extends Error`, carrying the original typed `why: Refusal`.
An error boundary may render it; callers choosing inline refusal UI use
`useQueryResult`, which returns `{data: R | undefined, why: Refusal | null,
read: Read<R>}` without throwing. These hooks do not substitute an empty list for loading/refusal. They add
no cache, previous-argument retention or observation ownership. `read` is the same snapshot as `useQuery`.

A data-only read does not promise completeness or freshness. It is for
screens that show the authorized rows that arrived. Pagination, absence proofs,
and actions depending on fresh or complete results continue to use `useQuery`
or `usePage` and their metadata. The precise API remains unchanged. Skipping
uses the existing typed arguments and `{skip: true}`. Required/mistyped
arguments still fail typechecking; result types come from generated operations.
`useMutation(op).run` is already a typed callable and remains unchanged.

Add `<SignedIn fallback={...} restoring={...}>...</SignedIn>` inside
AppProvider (bare SnapbackProvider is insufficient), using the same
`useAuth()` snapshot as AppProvider. Signed-in children mount only in that
state; restoring defaults to null, signed-out uses fallback. The existing
AppProvider account boundary resets account-owned state. Children must be JSX
components (React elements), not eagerly invoked component functions.
No bundled login UI or new session runtime is added to the React entry.

## 3. Completeness notes

Default check output leads with a checked repair against the author's own
query when the binder provides one. Print each distinct repair body once,
including different query names sharing one explanation. Otherwise print the
specific missing pin or the analyzer limitation, never invent a complete form.
The next line states impact: displaying returned rows can keep the query;
proving absence or all matches needs completeness and the precise API.
The final line names any audience proved complete. Verbose keeps full evidence.
Within one invocation deduplicate only identical findings (code, site, message
and repair), preserving different scans at the same operation site. Deduplicate
identical repair bodies separately. Recheck output follows the existing dev
watch lifecycle; no persistent acknowledgement is introduced. No persistent suppression
file, diagnostic acceptance syntax, severity change or new check exit is added.

## 4. UTC hour of day

Keep `hour(t)` as the continuous epoch hour needed by bucket keys and ranges.
Add `hourOfDay(t)` for UTC clock hours 0 through 23. It requires one present
time, returns int, and equals floor(t / 1h).rem_euclid(24), including negative
times. Lower it to existing Calendar and integer arithmetic; no new wire enum
or device runtime requirement. Index/group-key use is outside this addition
(the repeating clock hour is not a chronological key). Existing offset forms
of hour remain unchanged. Guide examples distinguish both at a fixed instant.
Clock cap/session changes belong to KIT4.

## 5. Sweep-only deadline advisory

Add advisory `N_SWEEP_DEADLINE` for a scheduled Quarry job which compares
now (or its periodEnd argument) with a row's time column and directly updates a string/bool column to a literal, when a mutation reads
that table and mentions a column in require/if which either the job updates,
or both the job tests and the mutation directly updates (the §8 coupling),
but has no direct time comparison on the corresponding row deadline. This
is a conservative syntactic warning, not a proof of a vulnerability or safety.
Name job, mutation, table and deadline. Explain sweep lag and ask for an
explicit comparison of that bound row deadline with now, with the intended
opening/closing direction and equality boundary. Do not invent a guard:
opening transitions and expiry transitions have opposite directions. Do not warn on
jobs without a schedule or on mutations already comparing that row deadline.
Limit claims to direct read/loop bindings and update expressions. Upserts,
int-coded statuses, read-filter-only tests, helper-mediated and computed
transitions may be missed. Suppression recognizes direct comparisons on the
same row alias, not semantic row identity; another alias or a helper guard
can cause a false positive. Any such comparison suppresses the advisory,
without proving that it enforces a deadline. FRONT owns this initial lint;
LANG4 owns unrelated notes and can maintain subsequent lint presentation. No runtime behavior or authorization changes. Tests include
positive, guarded, unrelated-clock, unscheduled, opening, equality-boundary
and unrelated-table cases.

## 6. Starters and qualification

Stop emitting recipes/production into ordinary projects. Package the same
recipe sources as build artifacts under node_modules/snapback4/dist/recipes;
the guide copies from that location when explicitly requested by the builder.
This is explicitly assigned to FRONT by work item 1, including permission
to remove starter-shipped recipe files; it changes no DAY5 adaptation behavior
or STAGE provisioning design. Existing projects keep any previously emitted
copies. New copies come from the installed, version-pinned tarball; integration
chooses the next package version without this branch bumping it. The existing
packed production qualification executes the exact guide commands.
Native smoke remains proof support owned by DAY5 and is attributed separately.
Every changed guide snippet runs from the installed pack; additive React hooks
get type inference, refusal, empty/partial data, skip, identity and subscription
lifecycle tests. Three evidence copies are rewritten and checked with the same
line counter without editing original lanes or dropping application features.

## 7. Review and implementation record

2026-10-18: Muse round 1 and fresh Codex rounds 1–2 found incorrect sweep
repair direction and loss of same-site scan/audience evidence. The RFC and
implementation now keep every distinct finding, deduplicate exact repair bodies
and repeated context separately, qualify audiences with the scan, and never
invent the temporal guard direction. Scope/version custody, syntactic lint
limits, AppProvider and identity tests were clarified. Fresh Codex round 3
and Muse round 2 both returned READY on the revised design and implementation.
Verbatim outputs with invocation provenance are under llp/reviews/3000.013.002-*
(the initial Muse stdout includes quota failure and successful key fallback).
This remains Review until implementation qualification is recorded; no author
acceptance or publication is inferred from the technical reviews.

## 8. Wave 16 source-repro correction: confirmation versus overdue

Read-only copies of the actual schemas showed that the first §5 trigger catches
020 releaseVehicle but misses 043 confirmItem. The wedding sweep tests
`not i.confirmed and now >= i.deadline` and sets `overdue: true`; confirmation
checks `not i.confirmed` and writes `confirmed: true`, but never checks overdue.
A status-only gate lint misses exactly the reported omission.

Extend the same advisory, without changing runtime behavior: after finding a
scheduled job's direct deadline comparison and literal string/bool update,
also consider a mutation which both mentions another field of that source
table in require/if and directly updates that field to a string/bool literal,
when the job also mentions it in require/if. This is a syntactic coupling,
not a proof that the job flag or guard belongs to the time comparison's branch.
The output reports the actual syntactic facts about columns, without claiming
that a condition controls or precedes the update or that two aliases are the
same row. It names mutation, job, alias and actual compared time field. The
sweep-written flag may lag; the mutation-written field is not called overdue. The same direct
row-deadline comparison suppresses it; no safety proof or direction is invented.

This catches a confirmation/overdue relationship while leaving unrelated flags
quiet. 046 acknowledgement already computes escalation using a direct deadline
comparison and remains quiet. Table-only conditions can correlate different rows
or branches, so the documented false positives and alias/helper limits remain.
Tests cover the coupled case, a direct deadline guard, an unrelated flag and a separated-branch correlation;
actual 020/043/046 source-copy results are retained in the report. The single
N_SWEEP_DEADLINE code and original exact-time semantics remain unchanged.

// @ref LLP 3000.000.000.001#8-wave-18-developer-loop-amendment-dx4 — bounded candidate scan, never an automatic script rewrite.
// Project-specific migration advice. Read authored files only; never print their contents.
import { readdirSync, readFileSync, lstatSync } from 'node:fs';
import { join } from 'node:path';
const excluded = new Set(['node_modules', '.git', '.snapback4', 'generated', 'dist', 'build', 'target', 'deploy', 'logs', 'store', 'output', '.runtime']);
export function upgradeWarnings(root, declarations) {
  const doors = [], persistence = [];
  let scanned = 0, incomplete = false;
  const walk = (dir, prefix = '', depth = 0) => {
    if (scanned > 10000 || depth > 8) { incomplete = true; return; }
    let entries;
    try { entries = readdirSync(dir, {withFileTypes: true}); } catch { incomplete = true; return; }
    for (const entry of entries.sort((a,b)=>a.name.localeCompare(b.name))) {
      if (++scanned > 10000) { incomplete = true; return; }
      if (excluded.has(entry.name) || entry.name.startsWith('.')) continue;
      const relative = prefix + entry.name, path = join(dir, entry.name);
      if (entry.isDirectory()) { walk(path, relative + '/', depth + 1); continue; }
      if (!entry.isFile() || !/\.(?:[cm]?[jt]sx?|sh|json)$/.test(entry.name)) continue;
      let size; try { size = lstatSync(path).size; } catch { incomplete = true; continue; }
      if (size > 1048576) { incomplete = true; continue; }
      let source; try { source = readFileSync(path, 'utf8'); } catch { incomplete = true; continue; }
      if (/\/seed\b|\/dev\/|x-snapback-persona/.test(source)) doors.push(relative);
      if (/\bstartDev\s*\(/.test(source)) persistence.push(relative);
    }
  };
  walk(root);
  const warnings = [];
  const passwordOnly = /^\s*use[ \t]+identity[ \t]+password\b/m.test(declarations) && !/^\s*use[ \t]+identity(?:[ \t]*(?:--[^\n]*)?)?$/m.test(declarations);
  if (passwordOnly) warnings.push('password-only dev doors are CLOSED since 0.4.33: /seed, /dev/* and persona headers refuse. Use deploy staging --staging plus serve staging for real users (guide staging); local fixtures explicitly opt into dev --unsafe-dev-doors.' + (doors.length ? ' Review: ' + doors.join(', ') : ' No matching dev-door scripts found.'));
  if (persistence.length) warnings.push('startDev() persists since 0.4.33: reruns see old rows and share the dev store. For disposable acceptance use startDev({args:["--memory"]}); keep persistence for continuity. Review (check each call for explicit memory): ' + persistence.join(', '));
  if (incomplete) warnings.push('migration scan incomplete (unreadable/large files or depth/file limit); inspect remaining authored scripts for /seed, /dev/*, persona headers and startDev().');
  return warnings;
}
#!/usr/bin/env node
// @ref LLP 3000.011.003.000#14 — resolve once, pin core and adapters to that same release.
import { upgradeWarnings } from './upgrade-warnings.js';
import { synopsis } from './cli-usage.js';
import { readFileSync, existsSync, writeFileSync, mkdirSync, readdirSync } from 'node:fs';
import { dirname, join } from 'node:path';
import { createRequire } from 'node:module';
import { spawnSync } from 'node:child_process';
import { previousVersion, installedVersion, acknowledgeVersion, compareVersions, installedHistory, runtimeChanges } from './release-changes.js';

let migrationWarnings = [];
async function run() {
  const args = process.argv.slice(2).flatMap(arg => arg.startsWith('--to=') ? ['--to', arg.slice(5)] : [arg]);
  if (args.length === 1 && args[0] === '--help') { console.log(`usage: ${synopsis('upgrade')}\nUpgrade snapback4 and every installed snapback4-expo adapter with npm, bun or pnpm; keep exact pins. Default: latest; refuses downgrades unless --to is explicit. Rebuild native apps after changing the adapter.`); return; }
  const json = args.includes('--json');
  const quiet = args.includes('--quiet');
  const input = args.filter(arg => arg !== '--json' && arg !== '--quiet');
  const explicit = input[0] === '--to';
  const target = explicit ? input[1] : input[0];
  if (input.length !== (explicit ? 2 : target ? 1 : 0) || (explicit && target === 'latest') || (target && !/^(latest|\d+\.\d+\.\d+(?:-[0-9A-Za-z.-]+)?)$/.test(target))) throw Error('E_INPUT: upgrade takes [--to <exact version>] [--json] [--quiet]');
  const log = text => { if (!quiet || text.startsWith('project ') || text.startsWith('Exact device')) (json ? process.stderr : process.stdout).write(text + '\n'); };
  let root = process.cwd();
  while (!existsSync(join(root, 'package.json'))) { const parent = dirname(root); if (parent === root) throw Error('E_UPGRADE: no project package.json'); root = parent; }
  const pkg = JSON.parse(readFileSync(join(root, 'package.json'), 'utf8'));
  const previous = previousVersion(root);
  const installed = installedVersion(root);
  const schema = existsSync(join(root, 'snapback')) && readdirSync(join(root, 'snapback')).some(file => file.endsWith('.q'));
  // Quarry declarations are whole lines. Scan every authored module; a comment
  // mentioning identity never turns a persona-only project into an account app.
  const declarations = schema ? readdirSync(join(root, 'snapback')).filter(file => file.endsWith('.q')).map(file => readFileSync(join(root, 'snapback', file), 'utf8')).join('\n') : '';
  const personaOnly = /^use\s+personas\b/m.test(declarations) && !/^use\s+identity\b/m.test(declarations);

  // Resolve in a fresh Node process: pnpm can replace the package symlink,
  // while this helper's module/realpath cache still points at the old release.
  const checkScript = `
import { createRequire } from 'node:module';
import { dirname, join } from 'node:path';
import { spawnSync } from 'node:child_process';
try {
  const root = process.argv[1], require = createRequire(join(root, 'package.json'));
  const cli = join(dirname(dirname(require.resolve('snapback4/bin-path'))), 'bin/snapback4.js');
  const result = spawnSync(process.execPath, [cli, 'check', ...process.argv.slice(2)], { cwd: root, stdio: 'inherit' });
  process.exit(result.status ?? 1);
} catch { console.error('E_UPGRADE: cannot load installed snapback4 for check'); process.exit(1); }
`;
  const check = (baseline = false) => spawnSync(process.execPath, ['--input-type=module', '-e', checkScript, root, ...(baseline || json ? ['--json'] : [])], { cwd: root, env: { ...process.env, ...(baseline ? { SNAPBACK4_UPGRADE_BASELINE: '1' } : {}) }, encoding: 'utf8', stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'pipe'] });
  const declared = pkg.packageManager?.split('@')[0];
  const locks = [['bun', ['bun.lock', 'bun.lockb']], ['pnpm', ['pnpm-lock.yaml']], ['npm', ['package-lock.json', 'npm-shrinkwrap.json']]].filter(([, files]) => files.some(file => existsSync(join(root, file)))).map(([pm]) => pm);
  if (declared && !['npm', 'bun', 'pnpm'].includes(declared)) throw Error('E_UPGRADE: supported package managers are npm, bun and pnpm');
  if (!declared && locks.length > 1) throw Error('E_UPGRADE: multiple package-manager lockfiles; set packageManager in package.json');
  const pm = declared ?? locks[0] ?? 'npm';
  const dependencies = ['dependencies', 'devDependencies', 'optionalDependencies'];
  const targets = ['snapback4', 'snapback4-expo'].filter(name => name === 'snapback4' || dependencies.some(key => pkg[key]?.[name]) || existsSync(join(root, 'node_modules', name, 'package.json')));
  const invoke = (command, capture = false) => {
    const result = spawnSync(pm, command, { cwd: root, encoding: 'utf8', timeout: 300_000, stdio: capture || quiet ? ['ignore', 'pipe', 'pipe'] : json ? ['ignore', 2, 2] : 'inherit' });
    if (result.error || result.status !== 0) {
      if (quiet && result.stdout) (json ? process.stderr : process.stdout).write(result.stdout);
      if (quiet && result.stderr) process.stderr.write(result.stderr);
      throw Error(`E_UPGRADE: ${pm} ${command[0]} failed; check registry/tool availability`);
    }
    return result.stdout;
  };
  let version = target ?? 'latest';
  if (version === 'latest') {
    const text = invoke(pm === 'bun' ? ['info', 'snapback4@latest', 'version', '--json'] : ['view', 'snapback4@latest', 'version', '--json'], true).trim();
    try { const data = JSON.parse(text); version = typeof data === 'string' ? data : data.version; }
    catch { throw Error('E_UPGRADE: package manager returned no exact core version'); }
  }
  if (typeof version !== 'string' || !/^\d+\.\d+\.\d+(?:-[0-9A-Za-z.-]+)?$/.test(version)) throw Error('E_UPGRADE: registry returned no exact core version');
  if (!explicit && installed && compareVersions(version, installed) < 0) throw Error(`E_UPGRADE: requested ${version} is older than installed ${installed}; refusing a downgrade. Use --to ${version} to request it explicitly.`);
  // Check the adapter release before any install changes package.json.
  for (const name of targets) invoke(pm === 'bun' ? ['info', `${name}@${version}`, 'version', '--json'] : ['view', `${name}@${version}`, 'version', '--json'], true);
  const pins = new Map(targets.map(name => [name, version]));
  if (targets.includes('snapback4-expo')) {
    const info = (name, field) => {
      const output = invoke(pm === 'bun' ? ['info', name, field, '--json'] : ['view', name, field, '--json'], true);
      try { return JSON.parse(output); } catch { throw Error(`E_UPGRADE: registry returned invalid ${field} for ${name}`); }
    };
    const peers = info(`snapback4-expo@${version}`, 'peerDependencies');
    const peer = peers?.expo;
    const floor = typeof peer === 'string' && /^(?:>=|~|\^)?(\d+\.\d+\.\d+)(?: |$)/.exec(peer)?.[1];
    if (!floor) throw Error('E_UPGRADE: adapter Expo peer has no supported exact floor');
    const current = dependencies.map(section => pkg[section]?.expo).find(Boolean);
    const installedExpo = current?.match(/^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/)?.[0];
    // Preserve a newer compatible SDK patch; otherwise select the adapter floor.
    const expo = installedExpo && installedExpo.split('.')[0] === floor.split('.')[0] && compareVersions(installedExpo, floor) >= 0 ? installedExpo : floor;
    pins.set('expo', expo);
    const tarball = info(`expo@${expo}`, 'dist.tarball');
    const response = await fetch(tarball, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(30_000) });
    if (!response.ok) throw Error(`E_UPGRADE: could not read Expo ${expo} alignment manifest`);
    const unpack = spawnSync('tar', ['-xzOf', '-', 'package/bundledNativeModules.json'], { input: Buffer.from(await response.arrayBuffer()), encoding: 'utf8', timeout: 30_000 });
    let bundled;
    try { if (unpack.status !== 0) throw Error(); bundled = JSON.parse(unpack.stdout); }
    catch { throw Error(`E_UPGRADE: Expo ${expo} has no readable alignment manifest`); }
    const aligned = new Set(dependencies.flatMap(section => Object.keys(pkg[section] ?? {})));
    // Router's wildcard optional peers otherwise select an incompatible Worklets.
    if (aligned.has('expo-router')) for (const name of ['react-native-reanimated', 'react-native-worklets']) {
      if (!(name in bundled)) throw Error(`E_UPGRADE: Expo ${expo} has no Router alignment for ${name}`);
      aligned.add(name);
    }
    for (const name of Object.keys(bundled)) if (aligned.has(name)) {
      const range = bundled[name];
      const exact = typeof range === 'string' && /^[~^]?(\d+\.\d+\.\d+)$/.exec(range)?.[1];
      if (!exact) throw Error(`E_UPGRADE: Expo alignment for ${name} has no exact supported pin: ${range}`);
      pins.set(name, exact);
    }
    // The old Expo runtime may recommend an older core than the adapter needs.
    // Pin the adapter's Expo-module floor too, including newly required peers.
    for (const [name, range] of Object.entries(peers)) if (name.startsWith('expo-')) {
      const minimum = typeof range === 'string' && /^(?:>=|~|\^)?(\d+\.\d+\.\d+)(?: |$)/.exec(range)?.[1];
      if (!minimum) throw Error(`E_UPGRADE: adapter peer ${name} has no supported exact floor`);
      if (!pins.has(name) || compareVersions(pins.get(name), minimum) < 0) pins.set(name, minimum);
    }
    if (!quiet) log(`upgrade plan: snapback4/snapback4-expo → ${version}; expo ${current ?? '(absent)'} → ${expo}; align ${[...pins].filter(([name]) => !targets.includes(name)).map(([name, pin]) => `${name}@${pin}`).join(', ')}`);
  }
  const warnings = migrationWarnings = compareVersions(version, "0.4.33") >= 0 && (!installed || compareVersions(installed, version) < 0) ? upgradeWarnings(root, declarations) : [];
  for (const warning of warnings) process.stderr.write(`project ${pkg.name ?? root}: upgrade warning: ${warning}\n`);
  if (previous) acknowledgeVersion(root, previous);
  if (schema && installed === previous) {
    // A previous package may predate snapshots. Capture its own compiler output
    // before install; never infer old facts using the newly installed engine.
    const old = check(true);
    let facts;
    try { facts = JSON.parse(old.stdout); } catch { /* Unavailable baseline remains explicit. */ }
    const api = join(root, 'snapback/generated/api.ts');
    if (facts && existsSync(api) && old.status === 0) {
      const counts = values => (values ?? []).reduce((out, value) => { out[value.code] = (out[value.code] ?? 0) + 1; return out; }, {});
      const require = createRequire(join(root, 'package.json'));
      const version = JSON.parse(readFileSync(join(dirname(dirname(require.resolve('snapback4/bin-path'))), 'package.json'), 'utf8')).version;
      const sources = readdirSync(join(root, 'snapback')).filter(file => file.endsWith('.q')).sort((a, b) => a === 'schema.q' ? -1 : b === 'schema.q' ? 1 : a.localeCompare(b)).map(file => [file, readFileSync(join(root, 'snapback', file), 'utf8')]);
      mkdirSync(join(root, '.snapback4'), { recursive: true });
      writeFileSync(join(root, '.snapback4/check-surface.json'), JSON.stringify({ version, sources, api: readFileSync(api, 'utf8'), notes: counts(facts.notes), refusals: counts(facts.problems) }));
    } else {
      if (previous) {
        mkdirSync(join(root, '.snapback4'), { recursive: true });
        writeFileSync(join(root, '.snapback4/upgrade-version.json'), JSON.stringify({ version: previous }));
      }
      log(`upgrade: old check did not complete; ${previous ? 'runtime history is still available from the previous package version' : 'previous package version is unavailable; see guide changes'}`);
    }
  }
  if (targets.includes('snapback4-expo')) {
  // Write the complete plan before resolving: peers may live in different sections.
  for (const [name, pin] of pins) {
    const sections = dependencies.filter(key => pkg[key]?.[name]);
    if (sections.length > 1) throw Error(`E_UPGRADE: ${name} occurs in multiple dependency sections; consolidate it first`);
    const section = sections[0] ?? 'dependencies';
    (pkg[section] ??= {})[name] = pin;
  }
  writeFileSync(join(root, 'package.json'), JSON.stringify(pkg, null, 2) + '\n');
  invoke(['install', ...(pm === 'pnpm' ? ['--no-frozen-lockfile'] : [])]);
  } else {
  // Preserve each dependency section. One resolved version, even across sections.
  const groups = new Map();
  for (const name of targets) {
    const sections = dependencies.filter(key => pkg[key]?.[name]);
    if (sections.length > 1) throw Error(`E_UPGRADE: ${name} occurs in multiple dependency sections; consolidate it first`);
    const section = sections[0] ?? 'dependencies';
    if (!groups.has(section)) groups.set(section, []);
    groups.get(section).push(`${name}@${version}`);
  }
  for (const [section, packages] of groups) {
    const mode = section === 'devDependencies' ? (pm === 'bun' ? '--dev' : '--save-dev') : section === 'optionalDependencies' ? (pm === 'bun' ? '--optional' : '--save-optional') : null;
    invoke([pm === 'npm' ? 'install' : 'add', pm === 'bun' ? '--exact' : '--save-exact', ...(mode ? [mode] : []), ...packages]);
  }
  }
  const after = JSON.parse(readFileSync(join(root, 'package.json'), 'utf8'));
  for (const [name, pin] of pins) if (!dependencies.some(key => after[key]?.[name] === pin)) throw Error(`E_UPGRADE: ${name} was not pinned to ${pin}`);
  const exact = existsSync(join(root, 'exact.mjs')) || existsSync(join(root, 'exact.json')) || dependencies.some(key => Object.keys(pkg[key] ?? {}).some(name => /^exact2?(?:$|[-/])/.test(name)));
  if (exact) log('Exact device rebuild: bun exact.mjs snapback --rebuild'); // HS owns this command and the pairing gate.
  log(`project ${pkg.name ?? root}: ${targets.map(name => `${name}@${version}`).join(', ')}; ${personaOnly ? "preview account adaptation with init --adapt --production; " : ""}regenerate with check, run acceptance tests${targets.includes('snapback4-expo') ? '; rebuild the native app' : ''}`);
  let history = '', checkedFacts = null;
  if (!schema) {
    try {
      history = previous ? runtimeChanges(installedHistory(root), previous, version) : '';
      if (history && !quiet) (json ? process.stderr : process.stdout).write(history);
      acknowledgeVersion(root, version);
    } catch { log('runtime history unavailable in installed package; run snapback4 guide changes'); }
  }
  if (schema) {
    const checked = check();
    if (checked.stderr && (!quiet || checked.status !== 0)) process.stderr.write(checked.stderr);
    if (json) {
      try { checkedFacts = JSON.parse(checked.stdout); }
      catch { if (checked.stdout && (checked.error || checked.status !== 0)) process.stderr.write(checked.stdout); }
    }
    else if (checked.stdout && (!quiet || checked.status !== 0)) process.stdout.write(checked.stdout);
    if (checked.error || checked.status !== 0) { const error = Error(`E_UPGRADE: packages pinned to ${version}; post-upgrade check refused. Repair the reported schema/device issues and run check again.`); error.check = checkedFacts; throw error; }
  }
  if (json) console.log(JSON.stringify({ ok: true, version, targets, packageManager: pm, warnings, check: checkedFacts }));
  if (!quiet) log(`upgrade: ${targets.join(', ')} pinned to ${version} with ${pm}; commit the lockfile, run check and acceptance tests${targets.includes('snapback4-expo') ? ', and rebuild the native app' : ''}`);
}

/** Own the app outside render; changing accounts replaces the client context. */
export function AppProvider({ app, children }: { app: App; children: ReactNode }) {

  const [boundary, setBoundary] = useState(() => ({ app, generation: 0 }));
  // Account identity is state, never a memo cache that React may discard.
  if (boundary.app !== app) setBoundary({ app, generation: boundary.generation + 1 });
  return <AppContext.Provider value={app}><ClientContext.Provider value={app.client}>
    <AppAccount key={`${boundary.generation}:${snapshot.viewer ?? ""}`}>{children}</AppAccount>
  </ClientContext.Provider></AppContext.Provider>;
}

/** The current account has opened successfully. Once ready, release switches
 * and later admission warnings do not unmount its shell. This is restoration
 * readiness, not continuing write admission, network availability or permission.
 * @ref LLP 3000.011.003.000.001#2-readiness-and-current-authority — drafts have an account lifetime.
 */
export function useAppReady(): boolean {
  const app = useContext(AppContext);
  if (!app) throw new Error("useAppReady: no <AppProvider> above this component");
  const auth = useSyncExternalStore(app.auth.onChange, app.auth.getSnapshot, app.auth.getSnapshot);
  const [opened, setOpened] = useState<App | null>(null);
  useEffect(() => {
    let active = true;
    const finished = () => { if (active) setOpened(app); };
    void app.ready.then(finished, finished);
    return () => { active = false; };
  }, [app]);
  const [admitted, setAdmitted] = useState<{app: App; viewer: string} | null>(null);
  const signedIn = opened === app && auth.state === "signed-in" && auth.viewer !== null;
  const initial = signedIn && !auth.why?.code.startsWith("E_ADMISSION");
  const sameAccount = signedIn && admitted?.app === app && admitted.viewer === auth.viewer;
  // Render-time state adjustment retains the first successful opening even if
  // React batches the next release notification before an effect could run.
  if (initial && !sameAccount) setAdmitted({app, viewer: auth.viewer!});
  else if (!signedIn && admitted !== null) setAdmitted(null);
  return initial || sameAccount;
}
